rv.q: This harrowing, tough-minded musical about mental illness, trauma, love and family is a genuinely courageous attempt to expand the form.
Where this show unambiguously succeeds is in its sympathetic but clear-sighted depiction of a family buckling under buried grief and an impossible present.
As art, it's problematic; as entertainment, it's first-rate.
Michael Longhurst’s production is sympathetically and sumptuously staged.

The sheer emotional punch which the production delivers from the get-go, with powerhouse performances from every member of the superb cast, is a testament to the strength and quality of the groundbreaking exploration on which they have embarked.
This courageous and deeply moving piece provides ecstasy as well as agony, light as well as darkness.
Equal parts heartbreaking and heart-wrenching, Next to Normal is the kind of show that you're left thinking about long after you've left the theatre.
Kitt and Yorkey’s musical soars in the hands of such an accomplished and connected cast.
Next to Normal has deep emotional resonance, wells of empathy that will grip you in individual scenes but it also has a notable cumulative effect.
It is a genius performance that carries the show, burning a mark of unsettledness into our brains, with many unanswered questions hovering into the night and wounds left gaping wide open.
The material itself still has shortcomings – its treatment of mental illness feels more slapdash and non-...
The musical, bold in conception, skilled in execution and acclaimed with modern theatre’s greatest accolade, a tearful standing ovation, has delivered.
The creative elements here are impossible to enthuse about: lightweight characters, flimsy music, forgettable costumes.
This West End transfer of Next to Normal proves that the show’s power to move and enlighten audiences has not diminished.
This is musical theatre at its very best.

In short, no matter your own backgrounds or experiences with mental health or grief, this story of an emotionally fraught family on the precipice of danger and longing for something normal (or even just Next to Normal) is sure to deliver an emotional gut punch.
Next to Normal is a resounding triumph in contemporary musical theatre, delivering a profound and unforgettable experience.
An absolute triumph, well-judged and delivered.

An astonishingly profound musical that expands on what it achieved at the Donmar Warehouse, Next To Normal is performed by one of the best ensembles in the West End at the moment and possesses beautifully composed folk rock music that remains timeless.
This new season of Next to Normal is one of the most anticipated events of the summer.
Michael Longhurst’s elegant production entertains and moves in equal measure.
Like Rent (also a Pulitzer winner) this is a musical that expands both the framework and vocabulary of its genre.
Brian Yorkey and Tom Kitt’s musical explores all the complexities that come of medicating mental health issues and coping with trauma.
In Next To Normal, Brian Yorkey’s book perfectly explores mental health’s impact on several members of a family with commendable, substantive detail – emphasised in Michael Longhurst’s direction.

However, it has to be acknowledged that this is a particular insight into the understanding of treatment available for illnesses of this nature and the Goodman’s are a white middle class family with seemingly endless resources to treat Diana’s condition.
Next To Normal is a faultless masterpiece perfectly portraying the soul-crushing effects of grief and mental health.
This is an emotional roller coaster on an epic scale that is not to be missed.
The experience is thrilling enough to make of it both enjoyable or worth.
Some might long for a little more subtext and others might suggest the musical is a tad too long.

cn.t: Critics praise this Pulitzer-winning musical's courageous exploration of mental illness and Caissie Levy's powerhouse performance, though some find it overlong and question its treatment of mental health. A raw, emotionally demanding show that expands the form.
